To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

DCs in lung cancer tissues and those conditioned by tumor-derived lactate are refractory to stimulation by endosomal and cytoplasmic sensors, and that this loss of responsiveness is due to downregulation of SNARE VAMP-3 and lactate-mediated inhibition of type I IFN signaling.

(1) Tumor-conditioned dendritic cells are refractory to stimulation with TLR3 and endosomal sensors, and fail to prime CD8+ T cells; (2) Tumor-conditioning induces downregulation of SNARE VAMP-3; (3) Tumor conditioning by lactate is sufficient to inhibit IFN production downstream of TLRs and STING; and (4) DCs conditioned by tumor-derived lactate fail to prime CD4+ and CD8

(1) Tumor-derived lactic acid suppresses the function of DCs in lung cancer tissues; (2) lactic acid suppress the function of DC by inhibiting the production of type I IFN and by accelerating antigen degradation; and (3) lactic acid inhibits type I IFN production by inhibiting the expression of the SNARE protein VAMP3.

understanding the mechanisms by which dendritic cells become dysfunctional in cancer and how we can use this knowledge to improve cancer immunotherapy.
understanding how the immune system can be manipulated to treat cancer.
the mechanisms of dendritic cell dysfunction in cancer.

we show that the loss of dendritic cell function is caused by the downregulation of SNARE proteins, and that the loss of SNAREs is caused by lactic acid in tumors.
the mechanisms that cause loss-of-dendritic cell functions in lung cancer are complex and multifactorial, and that the tumor microenvironment is a major driver for this process.
